column1: Hettie/s0|Did food tempt her?|Only if my aunt carried it. I had to earn her trust before she would follow my bucket.|Did your aunt want her back?|She visited often enough that the cow never had to decide between us.

Hettie/s1|Could Gwil take a turn?|He can manage the feeding. I would have to resist going out to check on him.|What would you do first?|Eat my breakfast while it was warm. A modest ambition, but there it is.
Hettie/e0|Has she escaped?|Into the lane once. I had to fetch her before a cart came through.|Could you close the gate first?|I do now. She waits on the wrong side whenever she can.

Hettie/e1|Does everyone bake that early?|Not everyone. But the people making breakfast have usually worked before the rest wake up.|What is your favorite breakfast?|Bread still warm enough to melt butter. Preferably eaten sitting down.

Hettie/h|Why did everyone help?|They all needed the same road. Leaving a broken cart there helped nobody.|Were the carts heavily loaded?|At harvest, yes. Unloading enough grain to lift an axle was half the job.

Hettie/w0|What if the harvest is poor?|The collector still wants his share. We make up the shortage from our own cupboards.|Can you ask for less tax?|We can ask. The man counting the sacks seldom has permission to leave any.|Who helps when food runs short?|Neighbours do. But sharing gets harder when every house has been counted the same way.

Hettie/w1|Will you keep more grain for winter?|Yes. Feeding the village comes before filling a royal storehouse now.|Who gets that extra sack?|Whoever needs it first. I know enough of our neighbours to ask quietly.|Does this mean less work?|The fields still need tending. At least we get to decide where the harvest goes.

Gwil/s0|Did the saplings all survive?|No. We checked them after dry spells and replaced the ones that failed.|Did he plant trees himself?|Every season. He could point to trees planted before I was born.
Gwil/s1|What does Hettie put first?|Anything that might let an animal out. A tidy shed can wait for a sound fence.|Who chooses the tools?|I do. She decides the urgency; I decide how to fix it.

Gwil/e0|Would a crooked hook snap?|Not if the grain follows the bend. A sharp kink or a crack goes on the fire.|What do you hang on them?|Light tools and coats. I test a hook before trusting it with anything heavier.

Gwil/e1|How do you find the loose joint?|I check where the boards move and listen nearby. The quiet makes a small knock easier to place.|Do you stop the mill to repair it?|Of course. I will not put my hands near working machinery.
Gwil/h|Why use different woods?|A repair often used whatever seasoned timber a neighbour could spare.|Can you tell who made a repair?|Sometimes by the joints. People settle into habits with a saw.

Gwil/w0|Why pay so little for good wood?|Because they can put a seal on the order and call refusing it disloyal.|Could the village run short?|Yes. A royal wagon takes timber we need for roofs and fences.|Does putting the fences first cause trouble?|It earns complaints. A cow through a broken fence causes trouble too, and sooner.

Gwil/w1|Which repair will you start with?|The bridge rail. A leaking shed is inconvenient; a fall into the river is worse.|Will you still sell timber outside Millwood?|When we have some to spare, at a price we agree to.|Could Hettie help plan the repairs?|She already has. Her list is longer than mine.

Odo/s0|Did anyone help you pull it up?|Two lads did. I heard about that bucket every time they crossed the bridge afterwards.|Did you keep the bucket?|Certainly. After an audience like that, throwing it back would have been wasteful.

Odo/s1|Did you ever compete over the catch?|Constantly. We just saved the arguing until we packed up.|What would you tell him now?|That the river still fools me, and that I wish he were here to enjoy it.

Odo/e0|Did a fish ever escape?|One slipped out of his basket. After that, counting seemed safer than trusting the lid.|Did you teach him to fish?|I taught him to bait a hook. He taught himself how to worry about the result.

Odo/e1|Why take the rod at all?|Holding it feels familiar. I can sit without people wondering whether something is wrong.|Do you ever forget to put bait back on?|Often enough to blame the fish unfairly.

Odo/h|What news came over the bridge?|Road conditions, births, prices. The things that matter before anybody calls them history.|Was there always somewhere to post notices?|No. People carried news themselves, and often improved it in the telling.

Odo/w0|Aren't you afraid they will notice?|A little. That is why I answer slowly and give them nothing worth writing down.|Who are they looking for?|They rarely say. I will not supply a neighbour's name merely to keep them entertained.|Why do they ask you?|I sit here for hours. They assume I ought to be useful to them.

Odo/w1|Have the patrols stopped asking questions?|Here, at least, people can cross without giving me an anxious look first.|Who would you like to see visit?|Calder, when his camp gives him a free afternoon.|Would you really leave your rod?|For company I wanted, yes. Do not tell the fish how easy it is.

Tolan/s0|Was carrying flour steady work?|Only when there was flour to carry. A guard's pay arrived more regularly.|Do you miss the old work?|The people thanked me when I finished. That is a difference I notice.
Tolan/s1|Can you refuse a bad order?|I can. Keeping my wages afterwards is another question.|Does shouting make people obey?|Often. It gives them less time to ask whether the order makes sense.
Tolan/e0|Are they still comfortable?|More than new ones would be. I mend them before a split becomes a hole.|Does flour ever come out completely?|Eventually. The smell stayed longer than the dust.

Tolan/e1|What might you miss?|Whether someone is hurrying to help a sick relative or simply late for work.|Do people mind being watched?|They mind being treated as suspicious for using their own road.

Tolan/w0|Why stop people without a reason?|Those are the orders. That explains them; it does not make them useful.|Could you let someone pass?|Sometimes. I cannot promise it when an officer is watching.|What did you expect guard work to be?|Keeping thieves off the road, chiefly. I did not expect to become another thing travellers feared.

Tolan/w1|Who gives the orders now?|That still needs settling. Until then, I can keep watch without harassing people.|Will you stay a guard?|If the work means protecting people. I still need a living.|Will people trust your uniform?|Not immediately. They remember what it meant before, and I cannot blame them.
Serjeant Bram/s0|Why did names matter to you?|An instruction reaches a man faster when he knows you mean him.|Did the recruits respect that?|They knew I noticed them. Respect took longer.

Serjeant Bram/s1|How did he keep a patrol safe?|He checked the route, watched the weather, and withdrew when staying bought nothing.|Is that how you lead?|When I am sensible. Rank makes it easy to mistake stubbornness for duty.

Serjeant Bram/e0|Do you remember them all?|Most. I ask again when I do not. Guessing is worse.|Why check their straps yourself?|A new recruit may not know what a loose fitting feels like until it fails.

Serjeant Bram/e1|What if someone hasn't returned?|We establish who last saw them and where. We do not start with accusations.|Do you count them yourself?|Yes. I sign the report; I ought to know whom it accounts for.

Serjeant Bram/w0|Do frightened recruits follow bad orders?|Yes. They fear the officer they can see more than consequences they have not faced.|Have you used that fear?|I have shouted men into line. I cannot claim clean hands merely because I dislike the king's methods.|What should a commander rely on?|Clear orders and trained people. Terror is a poor substitute for either.

Serjeant Bram/w1|Will listening be enough?|No. They must stop the behaviour they are being told about.|Will you listen too?|I gave orders. I belong in that conversation as much as any recruit.|What if people refuse to forgive them?|Then the men will have to serve without expecting gratitude.

Doran/s0|Why did the buckles matter so much?|Armor that shifts at the wrong moment leaves a gap. A polished breastplate cannot fix that.|Did you ever miss a loose one?|Once. The strap caught my arm during practice. My master made sure I remembered it.
Doran/s1|Did nobody else know how to cook?|Several claimed they did. Their porridge argued otherwise.|Did you enjoy cooking?|I enjoyed having something edible at the end of a wet watch.

Doran/e0|How do you avoid the burnt part?|Lift the good porridge gently into another pot. Scraping is where hope becomes a mistake.|Why not stop it burning?|That would require the man watching it to watch it.
Doran/e1|Where do you keep spare socks?|Wrapped inside my pack, away from the wet cloak.|Does wet armor rust?|If you neglect it. Drying and oiling are less glorious than charging, but more frequent.

Doran/w0|What does loyalty require of you?|Service. I am still deciding how much of myself I have mistaken for part of the uniform.|Have you challenged an order?|Not often enough to boast about it.|Would you lose your rank for refusing?|Quite possibly. That is why agreement comes so easily at court.

Doran/w1|Will you take the badge off?|Perhaps. It would not erase what I did while wearing it.|What do you expect people to remember?|The roadblocks, the demands, and the jokes I found amusing at their expense.|What will you do about that?|Begin by accepting complaints without reaching for my rank.

Elder Maddock/s0|Why take two maps?|They disagreed. I imagined carrying both would make me better informed.|Who gave you useful advice?|An innkeeper who noticed my wet boots before asking where I meant to go.

Elder Maddock/s1|Where would you look for her story?|Old records, family names, anyone who remembers hearing the name as a child.|Could the map itself be wrong?|Certainly. I would compare it with other accounts before treating it as fact.

Elder Maddock/e0|Why keep a ruined map?|It reminds me of that journey. A useful map and a valued keepsake need not be the same thing.|Did the rain leave you lost?|For an afternoon. I asked a carter for directions instead of trusting the ink that remained.

Elder Maddock/e1|What if both walked it yesterday?|Ask which route each took. The same destination does not mean the same road.|Would you trust the newer account?|Usually, but I would still ask what the traveller actually saw.

Elder Maddock/h|Who repaired the roads?|Local masons and labourers. A rider could keep danger away, but a bridge still needed hands to rebuild it.|Did everyone get to travel?|No. Money, weather and work kept many people close to home even then.

Elder Maddock/w0|Did you hear other accounts yourself?|Yes. People spoke more freely before repeating the wrong memory became dangerous.|Why would someone repeat his version?|Fear, ambition, or simply never hearing another. Those are different reasons, and worth distinguishing.|Where should I look for older accounts?|Thornwell's school preserves histories. Ask how the writers knew what they recorded.

Elder Maddock/w1|How do you teach it fairly?|Name what happened and who suffered. Do not make a child answer for a parent's allegiance.|Could someone hide the truth again?|Yes. Keeping several accounts available makes that harder.|What should people remember about us?|What you actually did, including the help you received. A useful history has room for more than its heroes.

Pip/s0|Can you hear someone standing still?|Not nearly as well. Weight tells me where they are; movement tells me more.|Do beetles sound different from people?|Very. A beetle makes a tiny scratching pattern, not those great thumps.
Pip/s1|Does it stay all day?|It leaves to feed. Cold evenings usually bring it back.|How did you notice it?|An itch beneath my cap, followed by a very determined little pair of feelers.
Pip/e0|How many guests have there been?|Enough that I stopped pretending the first one lived alone.|Can you ask them to leave?|I can shake my cap. It is a rather abrupt sort of conversation.

Pip/e1|Do you hear through your feet?|I feel the ground through them. The wet earth feels different from dry dust.|Does rain make the path easier to hear?|During rain, no. Afterwards, I can notice smaller movements again.

Pip/w0|What do you do when soldiers arrive?|Stay still and listen until the heavy steps pass.|Have they frightened you before?|Their boots have crushed caps near the path. I cannot tell which steps will turn toward us.|Would you greet kinder visitors?|Yes. I like questions better than shouting.

Pip/w1|Who was laughing?|Travellers speaking to each other. Nobody was ordering them to be quiet.|Were you still frightened?|At first. I waited before coming closer.|Did you speak to them?|I said hello. A small thing, but I had missed doing it.

Mycella/s0|What happens when a tree falls?|The roots remain for a time. I learn the changes before they disappear.|Could you teach me the route?|You would need landmarks you can recognise. My way of sensing it would not help your feet.

Mycella/s1|Did the dragons land nearby?|Not in our crowded ring. I remember them passing above the trees.|Could you tell them apart?|Some shadows were broader than others. I would not pretend that told me their names.

Mycella/e0|Does the old tree feed the new roots?|What decays returns to the soil. The next tree grows in ground changed by the last.|Can you tell how old a root is?|Not an exact age. I recognise growth I have lived beside.

Mycella/e1|Do you prefer shade or sunlight?|Gentle light. Too much heat dries us, whatever color the cap above us.|Do you sit with the younger ones?|When they make room. They ask questions I had forgotten to ask myself.

Mycella/h|Do you count years differently?|We remember seasons and changes in the ring. Your numbered years can help compare our memories.|Did the forest change after Wingfall?|People came through it more fearfully. The trees did not understand the new borders.

Mycella/w0|Has he tried to claim the forest?|His men act as though a royal mark settles who may walk here.|Was there a king before him?|Human rulers changed. The forest was never young enough to begin with one of them.|Can his orders reach the roots?|No. But his people can cut what grows above them, and that is harm enough.

Mycella/w1|Will the damaged forest recover?|Where living roots remain, some growth will return. Others must begin again.|Do you trust people more now?|I trust what they do here. A changed ruler is reason to watch, not proof of kindness.|What would help the ring?|Careful feet and room to grow. Neither requires a royal proclamation.

Bolete/s0|Why not cut the roots away?|Some hold the soil together. I clear enough room without tearing out more than I must.|Does the path stay open all day?|Usually. I check after rain, when the edges shift most.

Bolete/s1|You can sense what others are eating?|When the ground is wet, scents and traces travel farther through our ring.|Is sweet rot a treat?|Very much. You would probably prefer to keep your honey.

Bolete/e0|Could the path go around it?|It already bends around the largest roots. This one keeps reaching into the remaining space.|Does moving it hurt the tree?|Not if I loosen the soil gently. Cutting it every morning would be worse.

Bolete/e1|What if I step on a cap?|Move your foot without grinding it in. Some recover; some do not.|Do carts use this path?|The narrower stretches are for feet. Wheels do more damage than a careful walker.

Bolete/w0|Did the king's mark stop the damage?|It excused it to them. The crushed caps could not read the seal.|Did they listen when you objected?|No. They treated the shortcut as more important than what lived on it.|Why did they leave the path?|To save a turn. There was room to go around if they had cared to.

Bolete/w1|What did you plant there?|Small caps from the sheltered edge of the ring. They need time to spread.|Could another patrol ruin it?|They could. I hope people will object before the boots reach it this time.|Will you keep the shortcut open?|No. The proper path already carries people safely through.

Truffle/s0|Won't a leaf block the rain?|A loose shelter breaks the wind without sealing the ground. I move it when the weather changes.|Why tend the thin ground?|New caps struggle there. The sheltered places do not need me as much.
Truffle/s1|Did the fox ever wake you?|Frequently. It scratched and turned before settling again.|Would you let it return?|If it wanted the same hollow. I might object more firmly to the fleas.
Truffle/e0|Does another animal use the hollow?|Sometimes small creatures rest there. I do not require them to introduce themselves.|Do you miss that fox?|Its warmth, yes. Its scratching less so.

Truffle/e1|How do you avoid stepping on them?|I watch where I put my feet and leave the crowded ground alone.|Does shelter make much difference?|A dry wind can harm a small cap quickly. A little cover gives it a chance.

Truffle/w0|Do they see the caps at all?|Enough to step over them if they wished. They seldom wish.|Can you keep them away?|I can ask them to use the path. I cannot hold back a patrol.|What happens to the crushed ground?|Some growth returns. Deeply torn soil takes longer to hold moisture again.

Truffle/w1|Are the little caps growing again?|Some are. Others have not recovered from being trodden down.|Will you shelter the damaged patch?|Where cover will help. I must avoid pressing more weight onto it.|Do you still expect the soldiers back?|I still listen for them. Knowing the reign has ended does not end that habit.

The Shroom King/s0|What were they arguing about?|Where a path should cross the ring. Everyone stood somewhere the other route would inconvenience.|Did listening settle the argument?|It showed which concerns were real. Agreement took rather longer.

The Shroom King/s1|How do you keep the names?|We repeat them with their stories, so a name does not become an empty sound.|Would you remember an unkind visitor?|If the harm mattered to us. Remembering is not always an honor.

The Shroom King/e0|Who made the crown?|Members of the ring chose its shape. Low branches were not consulted.|Does the crown matter to the ring?|It helps visitors find whom to address. It does not do the listening for me.

The Shroom King/e1|Why wait until morning?|A tired argument can repeat itself for hours. Rest sometimes changes what people can hear.|Does everyone stay for the rain?|Those who wish to. A council need not become a prison.

The Shroom King/h|What if the quietest person is wrong?|We consider the concern. Being heard is not the same as having every wish granted.|Can the ring choose someone else?|Yes. The crown belongs to the responsibility, not permanently to my head.

The Shroom King/w0|Could your ring remove you?|Yes. I speak for them only while they accept that I do.|Has Halvard tried to command you?|His servants speak as though his orders apply wherever they can carry them.|Why call yourself king, then?|It is a word humans understand. I try not to let their worst example define it.

The Shroom King/w1|How should people choose a leader?|Ask whom that person listens to when agreement is difficult.|Could another ruler become like Halvard?|Certainly, if nobody can question or remove them.|Would you choose a human ruler for us?|No. I can tell you how our ring works. Your people must decide their own arrangements.

Calder/s0|Did you ever repair the cart?|Yes. By then I was using it to fetch supplies for the people stopping here.|Why did travellers keep stopping?|They could see a tended fire and someone willing to share news of the road.

Calder/s1|Do the fish stay out of the fast current?|They gather where they can feed without fighting it constantly.|Is it safe below the falls?|Choose quiet water with firm footing. Do not wade into the fast current.

Calder/e0|How do you keep it dry?|I choose sheltered ground and keep packs off it until someone needs it.|Do late travellers arrive often?|Often enough to make the space useful. Darkness catches people farther from town than they expect.
Calder/e1|Can a bad meal make a good story?|Especially when everyone expected a feast.|Do you tell your own travel stories?|I tell the cart story rather often. People look at the camp and ask for it.

Calder/h|Was a fire enough to start a camp?|No. People needed water, shelter and a reason to trust the person tending it.|How did you hear whether roads were safe?|Travellers coming from the other direction. I ask when and where they met trouble.

Calder/w0|Do travellers avoid the camp now?|Some pass quickly. Others stop only long enough to ask which way the patrol went.|What do you tell them about patrols?|What I actually saw, and when. Old news can send someone straight into trouble.|Has the king made travel safer at all?|Not for the people who arrive frightened of his own guards.

Calder/w1|Will more travellers be good for you?|More breakfasts to sell, certainly. Better still, fewer people too frightened to finish one.|Are both roads truly safe?|Open does not mean harmless. I still ask the latest arrivals what they encountered.|Would you travel again yourself?|For a visit, perhaps. I would need someone to mind the camp first.

Prue/s0|Was the nick his signature?|A private one. He disliked being praised more than he disliked leaving a mark.|Did he teach you masonry?|Yes. First how to judge a stone, then how to persuade it to fit.

Prue/s1|Why keep the tools wrapped?|Using them made his absence feel new again. I was not ready.|Why did the first repair fail?|I had not seated the replacement properly. I took it up and started again.

Prue/e0|Do you shape it before setting it?|Yes, then check the fit. A stone that only looks right can still rock under weight.|What if it keeps rocking?|Find the high point beneath it. More weight on top is not a repair.
Prue/e1|What wears a step down most?|Grit under people's feet, over many years.|Can you repair it without replacing it?|Sometimes. It depends how much sound stone remains and how people use it.

Prue/w0|Did the clerk even meet your father?|Often enough to demand more blocks. Not enough to ask what the work cost him.|Could your father refuse the work?|Refusal to a royal order was not treated as an ordinary business decision.|Is that why you remember his marks?|Yes. Somebody should know that he made those stones fit.

Prue/w1|How would you record their names?|In the town's accounts, alongside the work and the payment.|Would your father have wanted that?|He might have grumbled. I think he would have read it twice.|Will you work on the repairs?|If my hands and the work are suited to each other. I want sound walls, not a ceremony.

Toft/s0|Why check your lamp so often?|A new miner can miss a weak flame or a bad fitting. They were watching for me.|Did the cloth help your boots?|Enough to stop the rubbing. I bought the right size when I could.

Toft/s1|Did selling supplies replace mining?|Gradually. There was more need for reliable supplies than I had expected.|Did you really divide your last potion?|When somebody needed it. I preferred everyone getting home to owning a full bottle.

Toft/e0|What else do you check?|The fastening and the fuel. Light matters only if the lamp keeps working.|Have you dropped one underground?|I have seen one fall. That was enough to make the handle my first check.
Toft/e1|What made asking difficult?|I did not want the older miners to think I could not manage.|Did they help when you asked?|Yes. They preferred a question to a preventable accident.

Toft/h|What kinds of marks did crews leave?|Warnings and work notes. They told the next crew what had been checked.|Could an old safe passage become dangerous?|Water can loosen stone. A mark records a visit, not every change since it.

Toft/w0|Who decides the quotas?|People counting carts above ground. The rock does not become safer because their number is large.|Can a crew stop for a bad roof?|They should. Under those quotas, stopping costs wages and invites threats.|Have the officials ever gone below?|Not far enough to learn what the men are warning them about.

Toft/w1|Would the crews agree on what is unsafe?|They can argue from what they see. That is better than a quota deciding for them.|Will work be slower?|Some shifts will stop sooner. Fewer injured workers would be worth it.|What should a foreman listen for?|Reports of movement, water, broken supports. A quiet worker's warning still counts.

Linna/s0|Do you buy anything that early?|Often bread for Maren. Shopping hungry makes the basket heavier.|Do the sellers compete with each other?|In boasting, certainly. Most will still help a neighbour unload.

Linna/s1|How did you start helping Maren?|Carrying market baskets. She found other jobs I could manage afterwards.|Do guests notice the garden smell?|Some mention it. Others are too tired to notice anything but the bed.

Linna/e0|Were you cold when she gave it to you?|I had come in chilled from an errand. She noticed before I did much complaining.|Do you help guests the same way?|I try to ask what they need before arranging everything to look impressive.

Linna/e1|Why do herbs linger longer?|Bread sells early. The herb sellers are often still packing their baskets at the end.|Do you prefer the end of the market?|It is quieter. I like the morning bustle too, provided I have eaten.

Linna/h|Does Maren give you a list?|For necessities. She trusts me to judge the bread and fruit.|What was the last unnecessary thing?|An extra loaf. It was still warm, which defeated all my sensible arguments.

Linna/w0|Are the rooms standing empty?|Some nights. It means less work for people who depend on travellers.|What stories do you miss?|Small ones about other towns. Not every visitor should arrive with news of a roadblock.|Do the patrols come to the inn?|They make their presence known. Guests learn to be careful about what they say.

Linna/w1|What needs doing in the spare rooms?|Fresh linen, airing, and all the jobs nobody notices until guests arrive.|Are you expecting visitors soon?|People are talking about travel again. Maren wants to be ready.|Where would you like to visit?|Somewhere I have only heard described across the inn's table.

Wren/s0|Could smell really identify every remedy?|No. Berta also taught me to recognise the leaves and keep careful records. Smell was one check.|What if you still weren't certain?|We set it aside. Nobody received a remedy just because I wanted to guess correctly.

Wren/s1|How did you realise it needed shade?|The leaves wilted in the sun even when the soil was moist. I checked what conditions that plant preferred.|Why keep trying with that plant?|It was a piece of a garden I remembered. I wanted to see whether it could grow again.

Wren/e0|Was the jar truly empty?|It looked empty. Her point was that appearances alone were not enough to identify a substance.|Did she often test you like that?|Yes, though she usually explained the lesson before my temper got involved.

Wren/e1|How can you tell whether it's healthy?|I check the leaves, stems and soil. Waiting does not mean ignoring it.|Could watering too much hurt it?|Certainly. Different plants need different care; more is not always better.

Wren/w0|Why treat the king's men?|An injured person needs care. Their uniform does not close a wound.|What injuries do they bring you?|Cuts, bruises, exhaustion. I hear more about orders than anyone asking whether they can manage another march.|Do they ever thank you?|Some do. Others are too tired to speak much. I do not require a speech before helping.

Wren/w1|Will you still treat former soldiers?|Yes. Their injuries do not disappear because their king is gone.|What would fewer wounds mean for you?|More time for ordinary illnesses, and fewer families waiting for bad news.|Are you worried about revenge?|Yes. Refusing care would only leave the next person with another loss to avenge.

Bevan/s0|What happens to bruised apples?|I set them aside from the sound fruit. A bad patch should not ruin a whole basket.|Can a small bruise spread?|Damaged fruit spoils sooner. Keeping it pressed against the rest is asking for waste.

Bevan/s1|What did you do with the rest?|Used what I could and planted fewer the next year. Generosity has limits measured in carrots.|Did you learn what people wanted?|Yes. I asked before arriving with another basket.
Bevan/e0|Were the little apples less sweet?|Not necessarily. I had confused size with quality.|Did you let her choose one?|Of course. She knew what she wanted better than I did.

Bevan/e1|Do people return your tools dirty?|Occasionally. I remind them before lending the same tool again.|What if a borrowed tool breaks?|Tell its owner. Hiding a split handle only gives the next person a nasty surprise.

Bevan/w0|Do the collectors pay for the produce?|Not what I would ask a customer. Calling it a levy saves them the bargaining.|Can you keep some good apples back?|I try to leave enough for the market. They count carefully.|Do customers blame you?|Some do until I explain. They are tired of hearing that the crown got there first.

Bevan/w1|Will prices change?|They still depend on the crop. At least a levy will not empty the best baskets first.|What will you do with the crown's share?|Sell it here, or keep what the household needs.|Does it feel strange to keep it?|I still find myself counting it separately. Habits linger after the reason has gone.
